title: Binary search on a million elements
prompt:
A sorted array holds 1,000,000 elements. Binary search compares the target with the middle element and throws away half of what is left, over and over.

In the worst case, how many of those comparisons does it make before it can answer found-or-absent?

Type the number only.
reveal:
20 - the count is ceil(log2(n + 1)), which for integer n is the same as floor(log2 n) + 1. Each comparison also removes the element it probed, so the range runs 1,000,000 -> 500,000 -> 250,000 -> ... -> 1 after nineteen comparisons, and the twentieth answers it.

The number worth carrying is not 20 but the shape: every doubling of n costs exactly one more comparison.

  n              worst-case comparisons
  1,000          10
  1,000,000      20
  1,000,000,000  30

That is why sorting once to search many times pays off, and why an index lookup stays cheap as a table grows: a billion-row B-tree is a handful of probes, not a billion.
